newsitem.title: USA: How many funds are enough?.
newsitem.headline: How many funds are enough?.

text.p: At last count, investors could choose from more than 8,000 mutual funds, with companies adding new ones to the roster every week. Not all of them are worth buying, but it's easy to find appealing funds -- so easy that investors often end up owning more funds than they need.
How many funds should you own? That depends upon a number of factors -- including how much time you have to manage your portfolio, and what kinds of funds you buy.

You can get away with only one fund if you want to minimise the time you spend on investment matters. All you have to do is find a fund that offers appropriate exposure to different financial market sectors.

For example, you could chose one of the Dreyfus LifeTime funds (800-782-6620; $2,500 minimum investment; no load). The funds consist of three portfolios -- growth, growth and income and income -- that hold a different mix of stocks and bonds appropriate for investors at various stages of their lives.

Some investors, however, prefer to finetune their portfolios. That might mean choosing a handful of funds that have especially good records in specific market sectors. Most financial advisors recommend that your portfolio include exposure to large company and small company stocks, with holdings in both the U.S. and overseas markets. In addition, you probably should hold some income-oriented funds -- perhaps including domestic and overseas bond funds.

You probably can create such a portfolio with four or five funds. But many advisors would argue that you have to diversify further within each market sector. For starters, you have to make sure that your stock funds are diversified by investment style.

A fund's style depends upon whether its manager emphasises growth or value. Growth managers tend to invest in shares of fast-growing companies that may trade at premium prices. By contrast, value managers look for bargains in the stock market, often buying shares of relatively slow-growing firms that are temporarily out of favour.

Since growth and value stocks tend to take turns leading the market, it makes sense to hold funds that invest in both types of stock. Thus, your equity holdings might need to include a large company growth and a large company value fund, as well as a small company growth and a small company value fund.
Similarly, you might want to make sure that your bond fund holdings include issues with different maturities and credit qualities.

The problem? By the time you finish choosing a fund for every sector and style, you might find yourself with a dozen or so different entries to monitor. Thus, most investors find that it makes sense to look for funds that can do more than one thing. Example: Gabelli Asset (800-422-3554; $1,000 minimum; no load), which invests in shares of large, medium and small companies. Manager Mario Gabelli's style combines elements of growth and value investing.

Among international funds, USAA International (800-382-8722; $3,000 minimum; no load) buys growth and value stocks in both developed foreign countries and emerging markets such as Latin America. The fund has posted roughly 70 percent higher returns than its typical competitor during the past five years, with around 20 percent less volatility.

Bond investors might consider a multisector fund such as Janus Flexible Income (800-525-8983; $2,500 minimum; no load). The fund's managers invest in a broad range of bonds with various maturities and credit qualities. Recently, its portfolio consisted of mostly corporate bonds. The fund has gained 9.5 percent annually during the past five years, versus 7.8 percent for the typical multisector bond fund.

Another simple solution: index funds, which cover an entire sector of the market. For example, Vanguard Bond Index Fund Total Bond Market (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no load) attempts to mimic the performance of the Lehman Brothers Aggregate Bond Index. Equity investors can choose from a broad range of index funds. One solid choice: T. Rowe Price Equity Index (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no load), which attempts to track the S&P 500.

Some analysts argue that you will not be able to outperform the financial markets if you choose too many funds in too many sectors. After all, the way to beat the markets is to make big bets on a single sector that does especially well. But finding the right sector is a chancy business; you might be wrong more often than you are right.

Moreover, even if you diversify among a broad range of different funds, there are ways to boost your portfolio's performance. For example, you can make modest adjustments to favour a sector that offers bargains. Better yet, spend your time and energy trying to pick the best funds within each sector. That way, you stand a chance of beating the markets without sacrificing the safeguard of proper diversification.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
